strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: practical computation of geodesic interpolation and extrapolation on latent manifolds of autoencoders, connecting the latent-space geometry literature (Arvanitidis et al., Shao et al.) with the time-discrete geodesic calculus of Rumpf & Wirth (2015).

The methodological pipeline is coherent and technically sound: the discrete path energy with constraint ζ(z)=0, the augmented Lagrangian scheme with careful discussion of rank-deficient multipliers and inexact constraints (citing established theory), and the discrete exponential map (11) derived from the first saddle point condition are all well-founded and build on proven convergence results (Rumpf & Wirth, Cor. 4.10 and Thm 5.1).

The learned projection Π_σ via the denoising objective (12) is a clean way to obtain an implicit representation of the latent manifold with unknown codimension, with a nice analytic characterization as a Gaussian-weighted barycenter and a quantified defect O(σ²); the parameter study on the toy torus (fig. 9-10) provides some quantitative evidence on dependence on σ, sample size, architecture, and noise.

The experiments span several distinct settings (discrete shells with isometric autoencoder, SVAE on motion capture with a pulled-back SO(3)^m metric, image data with low-bending/low-distortion autoencoder, and Pose-NDF as a distance function), and the appendix gives substantial implementation detail (architectures, σ values, data generation, algorithm 1).

The paper is clearly written, well organized, and honest about limitations (e.g., slight self-intersections remaining due to filter width σ, sensitivity of exponential maps to numerical inaccuracies, and open questions listed in the conclusion).
weaknesses: Evaluation is predominantly qualitative. Apart from the torus projection-error study, the main results (figs. 4-8, 11-13) are visual comparisons against linear interpolation, with no quantitative metrics (e.g., path energy, decoded-path plausibility scores, distance-based errors, or comparison to ground-truth geodesics on the real datasets). Claims such as 'our geodesics avoid self-intersections more effectively' or 'yields realistic decoded paths' are supported only by pictures.

There is no comparison against the most relevant competing methods, e.g., Sun et al. (2025), which also learns an implicit representation of the latent manifold, or geodesics computed via decoder pullback metrics (Arvanitidis et al.). The related-work discussion asserts differences in approach but the experiments do not demonstrate superiority or even parity on any shared benchmark.

A key practical requirement is underexplored: the pullback metric W_M requires exact/fast Riemannian distances in the data space (e.g., dist_SO(3)^m or shell distances), and the Euclidean metric requires near-isometric encoders. The conclusion acknowledges this, but it substantially limits applicability to general autoencoders (e.g., standard VAEs on natural images), and the paper does not quantify how much accuracy degrades when these assumptions are only approximately met.

Sensitivity to the choice of σ is acknowledged ('suitable values of σ depend on the sampling') but the heuristic for choosing σ in practice is informal; a sensitivity analysis on the real experiments, not just the torus toy model, would strengthen the evidence.

Novelty is moderate: the discrete geodesic calculus and augmented Lagrangian machinery are adapted from Rumpf & Wirth (2015) and Nocedal & Wright, and the projection-from-denoising idea is taken from Alain & Benggio (2014); the contribution is the combination and application to latent manifolds, which is useful but not a fundamentally new method.

No statement about releasing code or data is given, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed appendix (e.g., autoencoder training specifics such as loss weights for the isometric autoencoder are partially deferred to prior work).

strengths: The methodology is mathematically well-grounded: the time-discrete variational geodesic calculus builds on the established convergence theory of Rumpf & Wirth (2015), and the paper carefully cites the conditions (smooth manifold, Lipschitz metric, O(dist^3) approximation of squared distance) under which their discrete schemes are justified.

The idea of representing latent manifolds implicitly via a learned denoising projection Πσ (Section 4) is clean, is independent of the underlying autoencoder, and the derivation of the projection as a Gaussian-weighted barycenter with an O(σ^2) defect analysis is a nice theoretical touch.

The augmented Lagrangian scheme (Section 3) is thoughtfully adapted to inexact constraints ζσ, and the design of the discrete exponential map (functional (12)) avoids second-order differentiation of the projection and decoder networks — a practically relevant detail.

The evaluation spans a genuinely diverse set of settings: isometric autoencoders on discrete shells, spherical VAEs on motion capture, a low-bending/low-distortion autoencoder on images, and even a third-party distance function (Pose-NDF), demonstrating generality of the framework.

Appendix C contains substantive comparisons (Stochman, uncertainty-regularized VAE decoders of Arvanitidis et al., LAND density-based metrics), including timing measurements and discussion of conceptual differences, and Appendix A/B provide reproducibility-oriented details (architectures, σ values, optimizer settings, tolerances).

Limitations and open questions are discussed honestly in the conclusion (dependence of accuracy on sampling density and σ, need for near-isometric embeddings or fast data-space distances, robustness of augmented Lagrangians for inexact constraints).
weaknesses: Evaluation is almost entirely qualitative. The central empirical claims — that computed paths 'adhere to the latent sample distribution', avoid artifacts, and are 'robust' — are supported only by visual inspection of decoded interpolations (Figs. 2, 5-9, 12-14). No quantitative metrics (e.g., path energies vs. baselines, distance-to-manifold of decoded paths, reconstruction fidelity, failure rates across random endpoint pairs) are reported for the real-data experiments.

Robustness of the method to imperfect implicit representations is the headline claim, but it is validated mainly on a single toy torus example (Figs. 3, 10, 11); the real-data experiments never quantify how much the learned projection's inaccuracy degrades the resulting geodesics.

Several comparisons in Appendix C appear anecdotal and potentially favorably configured: e.g., the claim that the Arvanitidis et al. (2022) baseline 'leaves the data manifold and does not converge' rests on one toy example, and hyperparameter choices for baselines vs. the proposed method are not equally tuned.

The flagship discrete-shells experiment (Section 5.1) is somewhat circular: it requires an expensive classical Riemannian construction (PGA with discrete geodesic computations on meshes) to synthesize training data for the autoencoder, which limits the claimed practicality of the approach as a reduced-order tool for shape spaces.

Computational costs are non-trivial and unevenly reported: projection training takes ~10-12 minutes even on toy/low-dimensional examples, individual geodesics take up to several minutes, yet there is no systematic runtime analysis or scaling study with latent dimension or point-cloud size.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which, combined with many problem-specific hyperparameters (σ, penalty schedules, tolerances η*, µ0, µmax, architectures), hampers reproducibility.

The contribution is incremental in a technical sense: the discrete geodesic calculus is taken from prior work and the projection is a direct application of the Alain & Bengio (2014) denoising estimator; the novelty lies mainly in their combination and the augmented-Lagrangian treatment of inexact constraints, which some reviewers may consider narrow for the main track.

The relationship between the choice of W (Euclidean, pullback, KL) and correctness of the resulting geometry is only informally justified in practice; e.g., in the SVAE experiment the deterministic-mean shortcut and the choice of W_M are made 'for simplicity' without quantifying the resulting approximation error.
